desc:
A rotation of a string moves some number of characters (possibly zero) from its front to its back, keeping their order. For example, rotating "abcde" by two gives "cdeab".

Given strings s and t, return true if t is a rotation of s, otherwise false. The two strings may have different lengths, in which case the answer is false.

For example, "abcde" and "cdeab" give true; "abcde" and "abced" give false; "aab" and "aba" give true.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Trying every rotation of s and comparing it with t works, but costs O(n²) for long strings. If the lengths differ you can answer immediately.
Write s twice in a row, for example "abcde" becomes "abcdeabcde". Where do the rotations of s show up in that doubled string?
Every rotation of s is a substring of length n of s + s, and nothing else of that length is. So after checking the lengths, ask whether t occurs inside s + s.
editorial: If the lengths differ, the answer is false. Otherwise, a rotation by k turns s = XY into YX, where X is the first k characters. The doubled string s + s = XYXY contains YX starting at position k, and the n-length windows of s + s are exactly the n rotations of s. So t is a rotation of s if and only if the lengths are equal and t occurs in s + s.

A naive substring search could cost O(n²) on repetitive input, so for a guaranteed linear bound use KMP or the Z-function on t + '#' + s + s. Modern built-in substring search is also fast in practice. Comparing all n rotations one by one is the O(n²) baseline.
